title: Hydrocarbons
tagline: Alkanes, alkenes, alkynes and arenes: preparation, properties and the orientation of substitution.

overview.intro: Hydrocarbons are the skeleton of organic chemistry, and each family behaves according to the bonds it holds. Alkanes are saturated and comparatively inert, reacting by substitution; alkenes and alkynes are unsaturated and react by addition; arenes combine both behaviours, resisting addition because of aromatic stability while undergoing substitution under the right conditions. This chapter takes each family through its preparation, its characteristic reactions and its tests, then closes with the directing effects that decide where a substituent goes on a benzene ring — the part that connects structure to synthesis.

facts.value: sp^3 in alkanes (109.5°), sp^2 in alkenes (120°), sp in alkynes (180°).

facts.label: Aromatic stability
facts.value: Benzene’s six delocalised pi electrons give a resonance energy that resists addition.

facts.label: Markovnikov rule
facts.value: H adds to the carbon already bearing more hydrogens, via the more stable carbocation.

learningOutcomes: Describe methods of preparation and the characteristic reactions of alkanes, including free-radical substitution.
Explain addition reactions of alkenes and alkynes, including Markovnikov’s rule and the peroxide effect.
Account for aromatic stability and write the steps of electrophilic substitution in benzene.
Apply the tests that distinguish alkanes, alkenes and alkynes.
Predict ortho, para or meta orientation from the nature of an existing substituent.

blocks.text: Alkanes are saturated hydrocarbons with the general formula CnH2n+2 and sp^3 hybridised carbon atoms arranged tetrahedrally, so their carbon–carbon bonds are strong and their chemistry is dominated by one reaction: free-radical substitution with halogens. Laboratory preparation uses sodium on an alkyl halide in dry ether, the Wurtz reaction, which couples two alkyl groups; industrial sources are crude oil by fractional distillation and cracking, and natural gas. Substitution with chlorine or bromine requires ultraviolet light or heat to start it, because the energy of a photon homolytically fissions the halogen molecule into two radicals. The mechanism has three stages: initiation generates radicals, propagation converts an alkane into an alkyl halide while regenerating a radical, and termination occurs whenever two radicals meet. Because the steps are random, polyhalogenation is unavoidable and the products must be separated by fractional distillation.

items: Wurtz: 2CH3Cl + 2Na → CH3CH3 + 2NaCl in dry ether, useful for symmetrical alkanes only.
Fractional distillation separates fractions by boiling range: petroleum ether, naphtha, kerosene, diesel, lubricating oil, residue.
Cracking breaks large alkanes into smaller alkanes and alkenes using heat and a catalyst.
Substitution mechanism: initiation by UV, propagation through radical chains, termination by radical combination.
Reactivity of halogens: fluorine explodes, chlorine needs only light, bromine needs light plus heat, iodine does not react.
Combustion of alkanes is highly exothermic, which is why they are fuels: CH4 + 2O2 → CO2 + 2H2O.

items.text: Methane with chlorine in diffused sunlight
items.note: CH4 + Cl2 → CH3Cl + HCl, followed by further substitution to CH2Cl2, CHCl3 and CCl4.
C10H22 → C8H18 + C2H4, giving an alkane and an alkene from one larger molecule.

blocks.text: Alkenes contain a carbon–carbon double bond made of one sigma and one pi bond, and the pi bond, lying above and below the plane, is exposed and electron-rich, so alkenes react by electrophilic addition. They are prepared industrially by cracking and in the laboratory by dehydrohalogenation of an alkyl halide or dehydration of an alcohol with concentrated sulphuric acid. Addition of hydrogen gives hydrogenation over a nickel catalyst, of halogens gives anti addition of bromine with decolourisation as the test for unsaturation, and of water in acid gives an alcohol. Markovnikov’s rule explains additions to unsymmetrical alkenes: the hydrogen attaches to the carbon with more hydrogens because the reaction proceeds through the more substituted, more stable carbocation. Alkynes with a triple bond behave similarly but add twice, and their terminal hydrogen is weakly acidic, which distinguishes a terminal alkyne from an alkene.

items: Dehydration: ethanol with concentrated H2SO4 at 170 °C gives ethene.
Dehydrohalogenation with alcoholic KOH removes H and X from adjacent carbons.
Bromine water is decolourised by an alkene but not by an alkane — the standard unsaturation test.
Hydrogenation requires a metal catalyst: Ni at 150–200 °C or Pt/Pd at room temperature.
Hydration follows Markovnikov orientation, giving the more substituted alcohol.
Alkynes decolourise bromine water and give a white precipitate with ammoniacal silver nitrate when terminal.
Oxidation with cold dilute alkaline KMnO4 gives a vicinal diol and decolourises the permanganate, the Baeyer test.

items.note: Markovnikov addition gives 2-bromopropane because the secondary carbocation is more stable than the primary.
The terminal C–H is acidic enough to give silver propynide, a white precipitate that distinguishes it from but-2-yne.

learn.title: Benzene: aromatic stability and electrophilic substitution

blocks.text: Benzene has the formula C6H6 with all six carbons sp^2 hybridised and a ring of six parallel p orbitals holding six delocalised pi electrons, which is Hückel’s count of 4n + 2 for n = 1. The delocalisation lowers the energy of the molecule by about 150 kJ mol^-1 below the hypothetical cyclohexatriene, and that resonance energy explains the chemistry: benzene resists addition because adding would destroy the aromatic system, and instead substitutes, so the ring survives every reaction. Substitution occurs in three steps. A catalyst generates a strong electrophile, the ring attacks it to form a sigma complex in which aromaticity is temporarily lost, and a proton then leaves to restore the sextet. Halogenation needs a halogen carrier such as aluminium chloride or iron(III) chloride, nitration needs a mixture of concentrated nitric and sulphuric acids to generate the nitronium ion, sulphonation needs fuming sulphuric acid, and Friedel–Crafts alkylation and acylation need a Lewis acid to make the carbocation or acylium ion.

items: Kekulé’s two structures are resonance contributors; the real molecule is their hybrid with equal C–C bond lengths of 1.39 Å.
Benzene adds hydrogen only under pressure with a nickel catalyst, giving cyclohexane.
Halogenation: Br2 with FeBr3 generates Br+, giving bromobenzene and HBr.
Nitration uses HNO3 with H2SO4 to make NO2+, giving nitrobenzene and water.
Friedel–Crafts alkylation uses RCl with anhydrous AlCl3 to attach an alkyl group.
Sulphonation is reversible, which makes it useful as a temporary blocking group.

items.text: Benzene with bromine and iron(III) bromide
items.note: Bromobenzene forms with the evolution of HBr; no bromine is added across the ring.

items.text: Benzene with concentrated nitric and sulphuric acids at 60 °C
items.note: Nitrobenzene forms as a pale yellow oily liquid with the nitronium ion as electrophile.

items.meaning: Extra stability from a cyclic, planar, fully conjugated ring with 4n + 2 pi electrons.
Wheland intermediate in which the positive charge is spread over the ring.
Replacement of a ring hydrogen by an electrophile, preserving aromaticity.
Lewis acid such as FeBr3 that polarises a halogen molecule to generate the electrophile.

learn.title: Orientation of substitution in substituted benzenes

blocks.text: Once one group sits on a benzene ring it controls where the next one goes, and every directing question is answered by asking whether the group releases or withdraws electron density. Activating groups donate density into the ring by resonance or induction, raise the electron density most at the ortho and para positions, and so direct incoming electrophiles there — hydroxyl, amino and alkyl groups behave this way, with the halogens as the famous exception: they deactivating by induction yet still direct ortho and para because their lone pairs donate by resonance. Withdrawing groups pull density out, deactivate the ring, and leave the relatively least-depleted meta position as the target, which is why nitro, carboxyl and sulphonyl groups are meta directors. The practical consequence is that the order of introduction matters: a nitro group must be reduced to an amino group and later removed if the desired product requires it, which is how the classic benzene syntheses are planned.

items: Ortho, para directors: –OH, –NH2, –CH3, halogens, –OCH3.
Meta directors: –NO2, –COOH, –CHO, –SO3H, –CN, –CF3.
All activating groups are ortho, para directors; all strongly deactivating groups are meta directors.
Halogens are the exception: deactivating but ortho, para directing.
Doubly substituted rings are directed by the stronger activator present.

items.text: Toluene nitrates mainly at the ortho and para positions
items.note: The methyl group releases density by hyperconjugation, raising density at ortho and para.

items.text: Nitrobenzene nitrates at the meta position
items.note: The nitro group withdraws by resonance, leaving ortho and para most depleted.

keyPoints: Alkanes are sp^3 hybridised and react mainly by free-radical substitution with halogens.
Substitution has initiation, propagation and termination stages, started by ultraviolet light.
Alkenes are sp^2 and react by electrophilic addition across the exposed pi bond.
Markovnikov’s rule follows the more stable carbocation; peroxides reverse the orientation of HBr addition.
Bromine water distinguishes unsaturated hydrocarbons from saturated ones.
Terminal alkynes give a white precipitate with ammoniacal silver nitrate because of an acidic hydrogen.
Benzene’s six delocalised pi electrons give aromatic stability and favour substitution over addition.
Substitution proceeds by electrophile generation, sigma complex formation and loss of a proton.
Activating groups direct ortho and para; strongly deactivating groups direct meta.
Halogens deactivate the ring yet still direct ortho and para.
examFocus: Quote the conditions with every preparation equation; reagents without conditions lose marks.
Distinguishing tests must name the observation, not just the reagent: decolourised, white precipitate, brown solid.
Mechanism answers need the electrophile named, the intermediate drawn and the final proton loss shown.
Orientation questions: state whether the group donates or withdraws, then give the position and one example.

Species with an unpaired electron formed by homolytic fission.
Breaking of large hydrocarbon molecules into smaller, more useful ones.
In addition to an unsymmetrical alkene, hydrogen adds to the carbon bearing more hydrogens.
Stability of a planar conjugated ring with 4n + 2 delocalised pi electrons.
Electron-pair acceptor that attacks the electron-rich aromatic ring.
Cationic intermediate of electrophilic aromatic substitution.
Relative positions 1,2; 1,3 and 1,4 on a disubstituted benzene ring.
Substituent that lowers the electron density of the ring towards electrophiles.
Coupling of two alkyl halide molecules with sodium in dry ether.

questions.prompt: The reaction of methane with chlorine in the presence of ultraviolet light is an example of:
questions.explanation: Light splits chlorine into radicals, which abstract hydrogen and propagate a substitution chain.

questions.prompt: Which reagent distinguishes an alkene from an alkane in a single step?
questions.explanation: The alkene adds bromine across its double bond and decolourises the reddish-brown bromine water; the alkane does not react in the dark.

questions.prompt: Nitration of benzene requires concentrated nitric and sulphuric acids because the mixture generates:
questions.explanation: Sulphuric acid protonates nitric acid, which loses water to give NO2+, the species strong enough to attack the ring.

questions.prompt: The nitro group attached to benzene directs an incoming electrophile to the meta position because:
options: It releases electrons into the ring at the meta position
It withdraws electron density strongly from the ortho and para positions by resonance
It is too bulky to allow ortho attack
It forms a coordinate bond with the electrophile
questions.answer: It withdraws electron density strongly from the ortho and para positions by resonance
questions.explanation: Resonance structures place positive charge on the ortho and para carbons, so the meta position is least depleted and reacts preferentially.

questions.prompt: The hydrocarbon family containing a carbon-carbon triple bond and the general formula CnH2n-2 is called the __________ family.
questions.explanation: Alkynes undergo addition reactions twice and have a linear geometry at the triple bond.

questions.prompt: The extra stability that benzene possesses because its six pi electrons are delocalised over the ring is called aromatic __________ .
questions.explanation: The delocalisation energy of about 150 kJ mol^-1 makes addition unattractive and substitution preferred.

questions.prompt: State Markovnikov’s rule and explain its basis.
questions.answer: In the addition of a hydrogen halide to an unsymmetrical alkene, the hydrogen attaches to the carbon already bearing the greater number of hydrogen atoms and the halogen to the more substituted carbon. The basis is the stability of the intermediate carbocation, which follows tertiary > secondary > primary, so the pathway through the more substituted cation has the lower activation energy.
questions.explanation: The rule is a consequence of carbocation stability rather than an independent principle.

questions.prompt: Why does benzene undergo substitution rather than addition despite being unsaturated?
questions.answer: Benzene’s six pi electrons are delocalised over all six carbons, giving a resonance energy of about 150 kJ mol^-1. Addition would break the cyclic conjugation and destroy that stability, while substitution replaces a hydrogen and restores the aromatic ring in the final step, so the delocalisation survives.
questions.explanation: Aromaticity is the driving force: reactions proceed whichever path preserves it.

questions.prompt: Describe the laboratory preparation of ethene from ethanol and write the mechanism of its reaction with hydrogen bromide.
questions.answer: Ethanol is heated with concentrated sulphuric acid at 170 °C, when an intramolecular elimination of water occurs to give ethene, which is collected over water. With hydrogen bromide the first step is protonation of the double bond: the pi electrons attack H+, and the hydrogen adds to the terminal carbon to give the more stable secondary carbocation in the case of propene, or an ethyl cation for ethene. In the second step the bromide ion attacks the positive carbon, forming the C–Br bond and giving bromoethane. Markovnikov orientation follows from which carbocation is more stable.
questions.explanation: Dehydration is an elimination needing acid and heat; addition is a two-step electrophilic process through a carbocation.

questions.prompt: Outline how benzene could be converted to a product containing a meta-directing group, and explain why the order of steps matters.
questions.answer: Benzene is first nitrated with concentrated nitric and sulphuric acids to give nitrobenzene, a meta director; a further nitration then gives mainly m-dinitrobenzene. If instead the desired product were a para-disubstituted compound, the amino group from reducing the nitro group with tin and hydrochloric acid would be used, since –NH2 directs ortho and para, and the amino group can afterwards be removed by diazotisation and treatment with hypophosphorous acid. The order therefore matters because each substituent present at the time controls the position of the next one: a meta director installed first forces meta substitution, while an activating group installed first forces ortho, para substitution.
questions.explanation: Orientation is decided by the group already on the ring, so synthesis routes are planned backwards from the target substitution pattern.
